name: Mesogun
lead: A mesogun is a handheld, spring- or pressure-driven injector used in mesotherapy to deliver many small intradermal injections of a solution in quick succession, typically across the face.[1][2] It is used in aesthetic clinics to put hyaluronic acid, vitamins and, in some practices, platelet-rich plasma (PRP) into the upper skin, with the aim of a smoother, more hydrated and brighter-looking complexion.[3][4]

Mesotherapy itself was developed in France, where Michel Pistor is credited as its founder, and the French Academy of Medicine recognised it as a medical specialty in 1987.[5] Wikipedia describes it as an alternative-medicine technique and notes that cosmetic uses have mostly been studied through case reports rather than standard clinical trials.[5] Research specific to mesogun devices is small: a bench study of delivery behaviour, a randomised trial of a stamp-type microneedle injector for skin hydration, and case reports including an adverse reaction.[1][3][6]

paras: Mesoguns let a practitioner deliver numerous shallow injections without manually repeating each one. A 2017 report in the Journal of Cutaneous and Aesthetic Surgery described a spring-loaded syringe for multiple rapid injections, a related design concept.[7] A stamp-type variant carries a small cluster of microneedles that is pressed against the skin and injects the solution at each press.[3][6]

Traditional mesotherapy uses needles on a syringe, and a pressurised version uses an air jet to deliver ingredients without needles. One study cited by Wikipedia found that both approaches reduced fat layers, with the pressurised system giving better results.[5]

The French press coined the term mesotherapy in 1958, and the technique spread from France to other countries.[5] The stated aims are to nourish and hydrate skin, to target fat cells and to relieve pain from conditions such as tendonitis and arthritis.[5] Wikipedia notes that cosmetic uses have been supported mainly by case studies, and that a study of 10 patients receiving facial multivitamin mesotherapy found no clinically relevant rejuvenation benefit.[5]

A 2016 study in Skin Research and Technology compared a commercial mesogun, a locally made intradermal injector and manual syringe injection. Blue ink was injected into polyurethane foam and pig skin while a pressure transducer measured cylinder pressure and delivery time. All three methods penetrated foam without ink flowing back out. In pig skin, the commercial mesogun let ink leak out quickly on needle withdrawal, while the other two did not to the same degree. Pressure levelled off near 25 mmHg when the backward needle movement lasted about 1000 ms, and the authors concluded that enough time must pass between insertion and withdrawal for adequate delivery. They framed it as the first evaluation of the mechanism of transdermal delivery in mesotherapy.[1]

Solutions chosen by practitioners include hyaluronic acid, vitamins and, in some clinics, PRP.[3][4] A 2021 report described seven patients with corticosteroid-induced rosacea-like dermatitis who received two sessions of PRP mesotherapy before routine treatment,[4] and a 2026 case series used high-frequency ultrasound to assess PRP injection for facial photoaging.[8] These studies concern the injected substance more than the device. Stamp-type injectors have also been used to deliver poly-L-lactic acid.[6]

Skin hydration trial: a 2020 single-centre, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group trial in Dermatologic Therapy enrolled 60 people. Participants received hyaluronic acid or placebo three times across the face with an automatic intradermal injector using a stamp-type microneedle (Dermashine balance). Corneometer readings at 4, 8 and 12 weeks showed significantly greater hydration in the hyaluronic acid group. Skin elasticity did not differ significantly, and no severe adverse events were reported.[3]

Case reports: the seven-patient PRP series and the 2026 ultrasound case series noted above looked at rosacea-like dermatitis and photoaging respectively.[4][8] A 2022 case report described rosacea that worsened, with flushing and erythema, after intracutaneous poly-L-lactic acid injection with a stamp-type mesogun injector. The authors suggested a subclinical inflammatory reaction and advised that PLLA injection should be done more cautiously in patients with rosacea or other inflammatory skin conditions.[6]

Wikipedia's mesotherapy article reports clusters of skin abscesses and a mycobacterial infection in Australia after treatment, and says inflammation and swelling have been linked to the ingredient phosphatidylcholine. It states that problems in France were later attributed to unhygienic conditions rather than the treatment itself.[5]

Regulation differs by country. The US FDA does not control what practitioners inject, which is overseen by state medical boards, and in 2015 approved deoxycholic acid (Kybella) for submental fat. Brazil and several other South American countries have banned mesotherapy for fat removal. France banned its use for fat removal in 2011 and the Council of State lifted the ban that June.[5]

card.summary: Handheld multi-injector for mesotherapy that delivers small intradermal doses of hyaluronic acid, vitamins or PRP; device-specific evidence is sparse.
card.aka: Meso gun, mesotherapy injector, stamp-type microneedle injector
card.note: Cosmetic mesotherapy has not been tested in standard clinical trials per Wikipedia; infection clusters have been reported.

quick.overview:
A mesogun is a handheld device that fires many tiny injections into the skin quickly. It is used in mesotherapy to deliver substances such as hyaluronic acid, vitamins or PRP, mostly to the face.

Research specific to the device is limited to a lab delivery study, a hydration study and a few case reports.
quick.mechanism: A spring or pressure mechanism pushes small amounts of solution into the dermis at each press, avoiding repeated manual injections. A lab study on ink in foam and pig skin examined how the fluid is delivered.
quick.risks: Reported problems include a rosacea flare after an injection through a stamp-type microneedle and infection clusters after mesotherapy in Australia. Regulation of what gets injected varies by country.

chain: Handheld injector places many small intradermal depots
Hyaluronic acid or other solution sits in the dermis
Skin hydration and a fresher, smoother surface
angle.text: Practitioners use mesoguns to deliver hyaluronic acid and similar solutions across the face in one session, aiming at hydration and skin glow. In a randomised trial, a stamp-type injector delivering hyaluronic acid produced higher skin hydration than placebo injections.
